segments.caption: Roll a dice 60 times, and each face should come up about 10 times.
But six comes up 16 times. Is the dice unfair, or is it just luck?
The chi-square distribution answers that.
Here's the definition, in simple words.
Chi-square measures how far the counts we see are from the counts we expect.
And the chi-square distribution shows how big that gap can get, just by luck.
A fair dice, rolled 60 times, should give 10 of each face.
Here's what we got: 8, 9, 12, 11, 4, and 16.
For each face, take the gap from 10, square it, and divide by 10.
Squaring makes every gap positive, and makes big gaps count more.
Add them all up, and the chi-square score is 8.2.
But even a fair dice never matches perfectly. So how big is too big?
Repeat the 60 rolls again and again with a fair dice, and the scores form the chi-square distribution.
It starts at zero, with a long tail to the right. Its shape depends on the degrees of freedom: six faces minus one, so five.
For a fair dice, 95% of scores land below 11.1.
Our score, 8.2, is inside that zone. A fair dice scores this high about 15% of the time.
So it could easily be luck. No proof the dice is unfair.
Data scientists use it to test counts everywhere: sales across the week, or what different groups of customers choose.
So remember: chi-square compares the counts we see with the counts we expect.
A small score could be luck. A score deep in the tail means something real is going on.
Quick quiz!
Another dice scores 20, with the same five degrees of freedom.
Is it fair, or suspicious?
Suspicious!
20 is far past 11.1, deep in the tail. That almost never happens by luck.
